repro: POST https://api.darshya.online/api/v1/digest/unsubscribe with NO Authorization header and body {"userId":"not-a-uuid"}
Observe 400 (a zod validation error), NOT 401 — the request reached the handler, so the route has no authentication gate at all
apps/api/src/routes/digest.ts:31 registers server.post('/unsubscribe', ...) with no preHandler and no authenticateUser
Its body schema (digest.ts:25) is {userId: z.string().uuid(), reason?: string} — the caller names the victim
digest.ts:46 then INSERTs that userId into WeeklyDigestOptOut with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, and jobs/weekly-digest.ts:238 reads that table to suppress the send
The ids are in circulation: jobs/weekly-digest.ts:471 builds the email link as /account/digest/unsubscribe?u=<raw user.id>, and GET /auth/me returns the caller's own id verbatim
I did NOT execute the write against any real user id — that would mutate a record I did not create
findings.observed: The endpoint is anonymous and takes the target user's raw primary key as its only parameter, so anyone holding or enumerating a Darshya user UUID can silently opt that user out of the weekly digest. It is also one-way: WeeklyDigestOptOut is only ever INSERTed (digest.ts:46) or SELECTed (weekly-digest.ts:238) — no route in the API deletes a row, so neither the victim nor support can re-subscribe them through the product. There is no sensitiveRateLimit on this route either, unlike account.ts:178 and :287 which do carry it, so the user table can be walked.
findings.expected: A one-click unsubscribe link should carry a signed, per-user, single-purpose token (an HMAC of the user id and a secret, RFC 8058 style) rather than the raw primary key, so that possessing an id is not the same as possessing the authority to act on it. The opt-out should also be reversible — a re-subscribe path so a mistaken or malicious opt-out can be undone.
findings.evidence: Unauthenticated POST /digest/unsubscribe {"userId":"not-a-uuid"} -> HTTP 400 {"error":"Invalid request."}. A 400 rather than a 401 is the proof: the handler ran. Same 400 for an empty body and for no body at all.

Once the platform passes 200 orders in total, a merchant's own orders start dropping off their orders page silently, and a merchant whose last sale is older than the platform's newest 200 sees an empty page. findings.target: admin API error payloads (every /admin/* error that carries a `code`)
repro: GET /admin/users/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 with the ct+admin token and header Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9
findings.observed: The payload mixes languages - an English `error` and a Hindi `message` in the same object - and an explicit Accept-Language: en does not change it.
findings.expected: One language per payload, and an explicit Accept-Language: en honoured.
findings.evidence: The identical Hindi `message` came back for Accept-Language absent, 'en-US,en;q=0.9' and 'hi'. Cause: pickLangFor (apps/api/src/lib/error-i18n.ts:377-409) ranks User.preferredLanguage above the header, and apps/api/prisma/schema.prisma:178 defaults preferredLanguage to `hi`, so an account that never chose a language is pinned to Hindi. Routes that build their own error string stay English - /admin/users?status=pending returns fully English text - so the admin surface answers in two languages depending on which code path failed. Plausibly an intentional India-first default; filed as an inconsistency at P3, not as a defect.

repro: GET /admin/ops/kyc-abandoned with the ct+admin bearer token -> 401
read apps/api/src/routes/admin-ops.ts:136 - the guard is authorisedToken(request.query.token)
findings.observed: Five endpoints mounted under /admin/ do not accept the admin bearer at all (401 for admin and for devotee alike). They authenticate on a shared secret passed in the QUERY STRING (?token=...), which is recorded in Cloudflare/Render access logs, browser history and Referer headers.
findings.expected: A header-borne secret (Authorization or X-Cron-Token), or admin-bearer access, for anything mounted under /admin/.
findings.evidence: 401 with a valid admin token on all five, while /admin/dashboard returned 200 with the same token in the same run. No bypass exists - authorisedToken (admin-ops.ts:25-33) is fail-closed on a missing or wrong-length secret and uses crypto.timingSafeEqual - so the finding is secret-in-URL plus a namespace that implies admin-console reachability it does not have.

repro: POST /bookings/book -> 201, booking 5902e915-2406-4d6c-a42f-81d7830ec9b7 (BS-20260908-5EJ3Y), priceAmount 1152
POST /bookings/5902e915.../cancel -> 200, status becomes cancelled
POST /bookings/5902e915.../cancel again -> 409 'Booking cannot be cancelled in its current status cancelled.' (correct)
GET /bookings/5902e915.../cancel-quote -> 200 with cancellationAllowed true and refundAmountInr 1152
findings.observed: After the booking is cancelled, the quote endpoint still answers cancellationAllowed:true and offers a full 1152 refund on a booking the cancel endpoint will refuse with 409. Root cause: devoteeCancelAllowed() (apps/api/src/services/cancellation.service.ts:83) tests only hoursUntilSlot plus an early return for pending_payment; it never checks for a terminal status such as cancelled or completed.
findings.expected: cancellationAllowed:false with the refund figures zeroed, matching what POST /cancel will actually do. The endpoint's own comment block (routes/bookings.ts:1864-1881) says this flag exists precisely so the quote and the executor can never disagree — the LEG-03 defect. That guarantee holds for the time-cutoff case but not for the status case. Not user-visible on web today: app/bookings/view/page.tsx:856 gates the Cancel button on statusIsCancellable, so the dialog that fetches the quote cannot open on a cancelled booking. It is an API-contract defect that any other client (mobile, a retry, a direct caller) can still hit.
findings.evidence: GET /bookings/5902e915-2406-4d6c-a42f-81d7830ec9b7/cancel-quote after cancelling -> 200 {"bookingId":"5902e915-2406-4d6c-a42f-81d7830ec9b7","cancellationAllowed":true,"cancellationCutoffHours":24,"refundFraction":1,"refundAmountInr":1152,"feeAmountInr":0,"tierLabel":"Full refund (48h+ before)","hoursUntilSlot":873.4}

repro: POST /bookings/book with devoteeNames [{name: <10,000 characters>}] -> 201 Created (BS-20260908-DVZZN)
GET /bookings/79337475-93eb-4ab8-b0ef-44a82a9b8295 -> the stored name is 10,000 characters, untruncated
POST /bookings/book with devoteeNames [{name: '  '}] (two spaces) -> 201 Created (BS-20260908-KSR9M)
GET that booking -> devoteeNames is [{"name":"  "}], a booking with a blank devotee
findings.observed: createBookingSchema (apps/api/src/routes/bookings.ts:85-88) validates the devotee name with z.string().min(1) and nothing else — no .max() and no .trim(). A 10,000-character name is persisted in full, and a whitespace-only string satisfies min(1), so a booking can be made with no readable devotee name at all. The name is the sankalp identity: it is rendered on the booking page, on the pandit's job card, and in the WhatsApp booking templates, none of which have a length budget for 10k characters. sankalpDetails and specialInstructions on the same schema are likewise unbounded.
findings.expected: A .trim() before the min(1) check so two spaces is rejected as empty, and a sane .max() on the name and the two free-text fields beside it.
findings.evidence: 201 {"booking":{"id":"79337475-93eb-4ab8-b0ef-44a82a9b8295","bookingNumber":"BS-20260908-DVZZN"}} then GET /bookings/79337475... -> first devotee name length 10000. And 201 {"bookingNumber":"BS-20260908-KSR9M"} whose devoteeNames read back as [{"name":"  "}].

repro: POST /bookings/book with scheduledTimeSlot '99:99' and everything else valid
-> 409 {"error":"The selected time slot is no longer available.","code":"SLOT_UNAVAILABLE"}
findings.observed: A syntactically impossible time is reported as a capacity conflict. scheduledTimeSlot is only z.string().min(1), so 99:99 passes schema validation and is caught later by the availableSlots membership test, which owns the 'no longer available' copy. The devotee is told to try another time because this one filled up, when the request was in fact malformed and no such time exists.
findings.expected: A 400 with a format error (the slot must match HH:MM and be one of the offering's availableSlots), reserving SLOT_UNAVAILABLE / 409 for a well-formed slot that is genuinely taken. The request IS correctly rejected either way and no booking is created, so this is copy accuracy only.
findings.evidence: 409 {"error":"The selected time slot is no longer available.","code":"SLOT_UNAVAILABLE","message":"चुना गया समय स्लॉट अब उपलब्ध नहीं है।"} for slot 99:99. Contrast: slot '' -> 400 'Time slot is required'.

repro: GET https://api.darshya.online/api/v1/priest/bookings?limit=500 with the ct+pandit bearer token and header 'Accept-Language: en-GB,en;q=0.9'
expected the user-facing `message` in English — the caller asked for English and this account never chose a language
repeat the same request with '&lang=en' to see the English catalogue entry the header could not reach
findings.observed: The `message` comes back in Hindi regardless of Accept-Language. Same with no Accept-Language header at all, and reproduced on three different codes: INVALID_QUERY (/priest/bookings), FORBIDDEN (/temple-portal/dashboard) and NOT_FOUND (/priest/bookings/:id). Adding '?lang=en' DOES return 'One or more query parameters are invalid.', which proves the English catalogue is present and only the header is being ignored. Cause: signup hard-sets the language to Hindi (SIGNUP_DEFAULT_LANGUAGE = 'hi', apps/api/src/lib/i18n.ts:81, applied at apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts:516 and :1464; the column default at apps/api/prisma/schema.prisma:178 is also hi), and pickLangFor ranks the stored value ABOVE Accept-Language (apps/api/src/lib/error-i18n.ts:377-410) on the stated reasoning that 'a profile setting is a deliberate choice' — reasoning that does not hold when the stored value is a signup default the user never saw. Net effect: Accept-Language is dead for every signed-in account and only an explicit ?lang= selects English. HONEST SCOPING — this does not reach a screen today, and I checked why rather than assuming: packages/api-client/src/error-shapes.ts:103-111 lists FORBIDDEN/NOT_FOUND/INVALID_BODY/INVALID_QUERY in LOCALIZER_GENERIC_CODES and prefers the English `error` label for exactly these, and on the pandit pages apps/web/lib/pandit-api.ts:54 composes a string that apps/web/lib/friendly-error.ts:182 then flattens to English copy. So this is a latent defect in the localization layer, not a visible one — it becomes user-visible the moment any client starts trusting `message`.
findings.expected: With no explicit language choice on record, Accept-Language should decide; the stored value should only outrank the header once the user has actually picked a language.
findings.evidence: HTTP 400 with Accept-Language: en-GB,en;q=0.9 — body: {"error":"Invalid query","details":{"formErrors":[],"fieldErrors":{"limit":["Number must be less than or equal to 100"]}},"message":"एक या अधिक क्वेरी पैरामीटर अमान्य हैं।","code":"INVALID_QUERY"}. Verified twice, and against ?lang=en which returns the English sentence for the same code.

blocked.reason: Cannot establish a browser session without /auth/login, which the brief forbids. In production the auth context deliberately does NOT persist the access token to localStorage (apps/web/lib/auth-context.tsx:465 removes poojly_session outside the compile-time-dead demo branch), and the API's darshya_session cookie is host-only for api.darshya.online so it cannot be replayed against darshya.online (documented in apps/web/middleware.ts:79-90). A cached bearer token therefore cannot be injected into the page's auth state. Mitigation: the full data layer was proved instead — every portal API these pages call returns 200 with a correct empty shape for its own role and 401/403 otherwise — and all 15 page shells were confirmed to render server-side without an error boundary. What remains unverified is only the client-side rendering of those empty shapes.
